pass_a_gloss: 'In the heavens' cannot circumscribe God (smaller than heaven, body, divisible, corruptible): Johannine goings/comings prove local language must be read worthily; kenosis returns to fullness and guides ours; Jn 20:17 is mind-ascent. Gen 3:8-9 collapses literalism (footfalls, real hiding, 'Where art thou?'). God walks in saints as in Paradise; heaven is saints, Christ the Father's throne, the church his footstool; essence stays uncommunicated while effluence reaches creatures.
pass_b_english: But when the Father of the saints is said to be 'in the heavens,' we must not suppose him circumscribed by a bodily figure, dwelling 'in the heavens' — for God would then be found smaller than the heavens, contained by the heavens that contain him. We must be persuaded that all things are contained and held together by him, through the unspeakable power of his divinity. And generally the words, taken at the letter, which seem to the simpler to say that God is in a place, must be transferred becomingly to the great and spiritual conceptions concerning God — such as these in John: 'Now before the feast of the Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour was come, that he should pass from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, loved them unto the end' (John 13:1,3; 14:23,28; 16:5); and after a little: 'knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he came from God and goes to God' (Philippians 2:7); and after other things: 'You have heard that I said to you: I go, and come to you. If you loved me, you would rejoice that I go to the Father' (John 20:17); and again after other things: 'But now I go to him who sent me, and none of you asks me: Whither goest thou?' (Genesis 3:8–9) For if these are to be taken locally, then plainly so is 'Jesus answered and said to them: If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our abode with him.' (Leviticus 26:12)

But these things do not happen with a local passage concerning the Father and the Son toward the one who loves Jesus' word — nor, therefore, are they to be taken locally. The Word of God, condescending to us — humbled, as befits his own worth, when he is among men — is said to pass 'from this world to the Father,' that we too may contemplate him perfected there, returning from the emptiness with us, which 'he emptied himself' of, to his own fullness. There we too, using him as guide, shall be filled and delivered from all emptiness. Let the Word of God, then, depart 'to him who sent' him, leaving the world, and journey 'to the Father.' And the word at the end of John's Gospel, 'Touch me not, for I am not yet ascended to my Father,' (Genesis 4:16) let us seek to understand more mystically — of the Son's ascent 'to the Father,' conceived by us with holy clarity in a manner worthier of God: an ascent which mind ascends rather than body.

This, I take it, I have examined together with 'Our Father who art in the heavens' — to remove the low conception of God from those who think he is locally 'in the heavens,' and not to let anyone say God is in a bodily place (for it follows from this that he is also a body) — which draws after it the most impious doctrines, supposing him divisible and material and corruptible. For every body is divisible and material and corruptible. Or let them tell us — not idly fanciful but claiming to grasp things plainly — how there can be another nature besides the material. And since, even before Christ's bodily sojourn, many writings seem to say God is in a bodily place, it seems to me not out of place to set out a few of those as well, to remove all entanglement from those who, through boorishness, enclose the God over all in a small and narrow place, so far as they can. And first in Genesis: Adam and Eve, he says, 'heard the voice of the Lord God walking in the garden in the evening; and Adam and his wife hid from the face of the Lord God among the trees of the garden.' (Psalm 123:1) We shall say to those who will not come to the treasuries of the letter, nor even knock at first on its 'door,' whether they can present the Lord God — who fills 'heaven and earth,' who, as they suppose, uses the more bodily 'heaven' as throne and 'the earth' as 'footstool of his feet' — as contained by a place so small by comparison with the whole heaven and earth that the paradise they suppose bodily is not filled by God, but is greater than him in size, so as to hold him walking, with a 'voice' heard from the base of his feet. Still more absurd, on their view, is Adam and Eve hiding, for shame at God over the transgression, 'from the face of God among the trees of the garden.' (Ecclesiastes 5:1) For it is not said that they merely wished to hide so — but that they really 'hid.' And how, on their view, does God inquire of Adam, saying: 'Where art thou?'

We have discussed these things at greater length, examining Genesis; but now, not to pass over so great a problem in utter silence, let us sufficiently recall the 'I will dwell in them and walk in them,' (Isaiah 66:1) said by God in Deuteronomy. For whatever his walk among the saints is, such too is the walk in Paradise — with God hiding, and everyone who sins fleeing his oversight and falling from frankness. For so too 'Cain went out from the face of God and dwelt in the land of Nod over against Eden.' (Wisdom 7:25) As, then, he dwells in the saints, so also in heaven — that is, in every saint and in Christ, in whom are all the saved as 'luminaries' and stars of heaven — or even because of the saints in heaven he dwells there, according to the saying 'To thee I lifted my eyes, who dwellest in heaven.' And the saying in Ecclesiastes, 'Hasten not to utter a word before God, for God is in heaven above, and thou upon earth below,' means to declare the distance from those in the body — of lowliness — to those lifted by profit and the word, the angels and holy powers, and Christ himself. For it is not absurd that he himself should properly be the throne of the Father — allegorically called heaven — and his church, called earth, should be 'the footstool of his feet.'

We have added, then, a few sayings even from the old covenant, deemed to present God in a place — to persuade the reader on every side, with the power given us, to hear divine Scripture more loftily and more spiritually whenever it seems to teach that God is in a place. And these things had to be examined together with 'Our Father who art in the heavens' — as withdrawing, so to speak, God's essence from all generated things. For the things with which God's essence does not commune(?) receive a certain glory and power of God — and, if I may so speak, an effluence of divinity comes to be in them.
